claims.text: A W-V-Ta-Ti-Cr refractory high-entropy-alloy coating can be prepared on 42-CrMo steel by laser cladding.
The as-clad coating contains a solid-solution matrix.
The coating has the potential to form Cr-rich oxides and W/Ta-based refractory phases.
Sliding-wear tests should be conducted from 25 °C to above 800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere.
Wear resistance will improve as ambient temperature rises from 25 °C to approximately 600–700 °C.
The initial improvement in wear resistance is caused by activation of a protective, self-healing oxide scale.
At moderate temperatures, the coating forms a dense Cr2O3-rich scale.
A dense oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and lowers the wear rate through tribo-oxidation.
Above the critical temperature, brittle Cr- or W-based intermetallic compounds form.
Coarse oxide inclusions develop at high temperature and can act as crack-initiation sites.
Increasing temperature can shift deformation from dislocation glide to diffusion-controlled dislocation creep.
Diffusion-controlled creep and grain-boundary sliding reduce the bulk hardness of the W-V-Ta-Ti-Cr coating.
Brittle intermetallics and coarse oxides cause microcracking and oxide-scale spallation.
Scale spallation exposes a softened matrix to abrasive wear and sharply increases wear rate.
The wear-rate curve has a minimum near 600 °C and then increases exponentially above approximately 700 °C.
The room-temperature coating lacks the benefit of thermally activated protective oxide formation.
The performance-degradation boundary occurs at approximately 700–800 °C, when oxide-scale spallation and significant diffusion creep outweigh oxidation protection.
A creep stress exponent greater than 5 characterizes the proposed degradation boundary.
The exact transition temperature depends on Cr content and sliding load or speed because these variables alter oxide-growth kinetics.
Brittle intermetallic formation has not been explicitly quantified for the specific W-V-Ta-Ti-Cr coating in the cited evidence.

contradictions.description: The curve is described as either 'U-shaped' or 'inverted U-shaped,' although the subsequent description—wear rate decreasing to a minimum and then increasing—is specifically U-shaped.

The critical threshold is variously placed at approximately 600–700 °C and 700–800 °C, without clearly distinguishing the wear minimum, onset of degradation, and completion of the mechanism transition.

The hypothesis states that degradation involves a transition from diffusion-controlled wear to spallation and diffusion creep, while the mechanism section instead presents diffusion-controlled creep as a newly activated high-temperature degradation mechanism after the moderate-temperature tribo-oxidation regime.
